1:
The heir is weighed before the crisis is described. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) opens on the arithmetic of Solomon’s household: a thousand wives and concubines, yet but one son to bear up his name, and he a fool; sin is a bad way of building up a family. Nor did the son inherit his father’s wisdom, and then it stood him in little stead to inherit his throne, for neither wisdom nor grace runs in the blood. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) draws the same moral: had Solomon kept within reasonable bounds he would probably have had more children, and such as would have discerned the delicacy of their position. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) measure the loss: by this renunciation of the Davidic sovereignty the kingdom of God in Israel was rent asunder, weakening not only the political power of the state but the spiritual power of the covenant nation.

Where the coronation was held shapes the whole reading. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds a constitutional distinction behind it: David made a league with the elders of Israel when they made him king, which implies a less absolute royalty than the unconditional anointing over Judah; so Rehoboam succeeds without question to Judah’s throne but must be made king by the rest, with some right to require conditions first. It is significant, he adds, that the ceremonial was fixed not at Jerusalem but at Shechem, chief city of Ephraim, which became of course the northern capital after the disruption; and in an arrangement without precedent there was perhaps some omen of revolution. Henry reads the move as a trap: their pretence was to make him king, but the design was to unmake him, and Rehoboam, supposed to have known of the threatening that the kingdom should be rent from him, hoped by treating with the ten tribes there to prevent it, and only hastened the rupture.

How Jeroboam came to be there is a textual question. Ellicott reports that Chronicles and the Greek have him return from Egypt on hearing of Solomon’s death and be sent for from his own city, which is far more probable and might be read in the Hebrew by a slight change. Keil and Delitzsch describe the Hebrew as a complicated construction whose main clause is delayed by intervening circumstantial clauses, and treat the parallel account as simplifying it by changing that Jeroboam dwelt in Egypt into that he returned. John Gill (reformed) takes a middle course with Kimchi, reading the verb as a pluperfect, they had sent, which was the reason of his return. Henry thinks the errand needless: Jeroboam knew what God had designed him for and would have come unsent.

Whether the grievance was real splits the voices. Clarke hears two complaints, of laborious service and heavy taxation, and holds that at first Solomon used no Israelite in drudgery, but afterwards, forsaking the God of compassion, used them as slaves and revived the Egyptian bondage. Ellicott infers their right from the narrative’s tone and the king’s want of resentment: the burdens were against old traditions and even against Solomon’s own earlier practice, so asking their removal was compatible with a loyal willingness to serve. Against them, Keil and Delitzsch allow that Solomon demanded more than the people were accustomed to, for his court and his buildings, but hold that he secured them undisturbed peace and great wealth from the trade and tribute of subjugated nations, so that there can have been no well-grounded occasion for complaint. Henry presses harder: if the buildings cost them money they cost no blood, and when silver was in a manner as common as the stones they did but render to Solomon the things that were Solomon’s. Gill agrees on the sharpest point: the one grievance they had cause to name, the idolatry set up among them, is never mentioned.
6:
Taking counsel at all is credited, then qualified. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) grants it was prudent to take advice, having so weak a head of his own, but impolitic to have taken time to consider, since he gave the disaffected time to ripen a revolt, and deliberating in so plain a case would be read as showing how little he cared for their ease. On the advice itself Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) builds a theory of kingship: this is the constitutional idea of a king, servant but not slave of his people; the way to ensure obedience is to let the people see that the king lives for them and not for himself, since the king is made for the people and not the people for the king. Henry puts the rule in a sentence: the way to rule is to serve, and to stoop to do it.

Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) admires neither party: both policies show how corrupt and cynical the government of Israel had become, and the old counsellors’ advice has no largeness of policy or depth of wisdom. It is the advice of crafty politicians who had watched despotic power develop, still remembered the comparative freedom of earlier days, understood the dangerous vehemence of popular excitement and how easily concessions satisfy it, and perhaps wished to defeat the private ambition using that grievance. It is to give good words and be for the moment a servant, perhaps meaning to abolish some excessive grievances but by no means to yield up substantial power; whether it was more than superficially prudent would depend on how serious those grievances were.

Why the young men were consulted is explained two ways. Clarke reports the custom of educating young noblemen of nearly the heir’s age alongside him, which, as Calmet observes, excited the prince to emulation and taught him the dispositions of his future officers; the old counsellors Rehoboam did not know, while with the young nobility he had been familiar. Henry treats the preference as a symptom: days should speak, and it was folly to think that because they had been his companions in the pleasures of his youth they were fit to manage a kingdom; great wits have not always the most wisdom, nor are those our best friends who know how to make us merry. John Gill (reformed) looks to temper: the counsel did not suit his haughty disposition, he could not brook stooping to his people, and thought it a lessening of his dignity to do anything that looked like courting their favour.

The answer they framed is read as a style as well as a policy. Ellicott calls them the spoilt children of a luxurious despotism, of which alone they had experience, and their language that of an arrogant self-confidence which mistakes obstinacy for vigour and, blind to the signs of the times, supposes that what once was possible must last for ever; it is needlessly offensive, yet a not unfrequent policy in revolutionary times, holding that to yield at one point endangers the whole fabric of sovereignty, and succeeding only where popular disaffection is superficial. Henry notices the vanity of the drafting: the young men thought the old had expressed themselves but dully, and furnished the king with quaint and pointed similitudes, though that is not always the best sense which is best worded. Clarke reads the little finger as a proverb: as much as the thigh surpasses it, so much did the son claim to exceed his father in power. On the scorpions he and Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) agree with Isidore that they are whips armed with barbed points like a scorpion’s sting, Clarke adding that the name was also given a Roman engine for shooting poisoned arrows, and Keil and Delitzsch that the Targum and Syriac read a word meaning simply a whip.
12:
The answer is delivered in the young men’s own words. John Gill (reformed) has the king answer in a blustering manner, with hard words and severe menaces, worked up to that spirit by his young counsellors and speaking in the very language of their advice. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) counts the blunders. He fancied himself better able to impose on them than his father, not considering how far he was inferior in capacity; and he offered this provocation to a people whom long ease had made wealthy, strong and proud, and who would not be trampled on as a dispirited people may be. Behind it Henry sees temper rather than calculation: he would rather risk losing them than deny himself so far as to give them good words, and many ruin themselves by consulting their humour more than their interest.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) will not let the English of the next clause stand. Making the best of the present version, he allows that God left Rehoboam to himself and did not incline his heart to the wise men; but if we ask what the cause of all this anarchy really was, we find it was Rehoboam’s folly, cruelty and despotic tyranny, and asks whether that was from the Lord. The text, he answers, does not say so: the Hebrew word means the revolution, and none of the ancient translations took it as the present version does, rendering instead that the turning away was from the Lord, or that it was the Lord’s ordinance that they should turn from this foolish king. What God did was stir up the people to revolt from a man who had neither skill nor humanity to govern them; and Clarke adds that these nations had such a revolution in 1688 and have never since needed another.

Two voices meet the same clause without disturbing it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes it as a standing instance of the great mystery of life, the reconcilement of an all-ordaining providence with the freedom, and therefore the folly and sin, of man; and he observes that Scripture, here confirming natural reason, simply recognises both powers as real without any attempt to harmonise them. Rehoboam’s folly and arrogance worked out the ordained judgment of God, but they were folly and arrogance still. Henry says it with the emphasis reversed: God left him to his own folly and hid from his eyes the things which belonged to his peace, serving his own righteous purposes by the imprudences of men and snaring sinners in the work of their own hands.

The cry that breaks up the assembly is older than the quarrel. Ellicott notes that it had been heard before, in the conflict between Judah and Israel after the earlier rebellion, where Joab’s relentless promptitude silenced it instantly; only the last ironical line is new, see to thine own house, David, in which he hears a sarcastic allusion to the promise to establish that house — be a king, but only in thine own house. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) draw the political conclusion: the words, with which Sheba had once preached rebellion, express a deep-rooted aversion to the Davidic monarchy so unvarnished that we may clearly see there were deeper causes for the secession than the pretended oppression of Solomon’s government, its real foundation being the ancient jealousy of the tribes, which David and Solomon had only suppressed for a time. Henry is torn: they spoke very unbecomingly of the great benefactor of their nation, calling him no greater a man than his neighbours, and their resolution was rash, since asking who gave Rehoboam his advice and removing those counsellors might have prevented the rupture; yet their jealousy for liberty and property well became that free people, who are willing to be ruled but not to be ridden.
17:
Who was left to Rehoboam is a question of geography. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) calls the phrase significant: historically Judah had its semi-dependent tribes — Simeon already absorbed into it, Dan in great part transferred to the extreme north, Benjamin closely united to it by the position of Jerusalem — so that the southern territory would be really the Judaea of later times. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read them as members of the ten tribes settled in Judah over the ages, the Simeonites especially, whose territory obliged them to remain; and they insist the verse cannot mean, as Ewald had it, that the tribe of Judah declared for its countryman.

The embassy that followed is judged the worst step of all. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supposes Adoram sent to collect the ordinary taxes, and calls the sending of him, with the public mind in such fermentation, another proof of Rehoboam’s incapacity; the people, indignant at the master who gave them such a brutish answer, stoned the servant. Keil and Delitzsch read the errand more charitably, as an attempt to appease the tribes and open negotiations, given to the superintendent of the tribute because the burdens complained of were his department, the king being no doubt serious in his wish to meet their demands; but sending this man only increased the bitterness, and Rehoboam had to summon all his strength to escape by flight to his chariot. Ellicott adds that the officer must be the one who held the post under Solomon, the name and office probably hereditary, and that the sight of their old taskmaster stirred the multitude to a fresh burst of fury.

Whether the revolt was lawful is answered three ways. Clarke denies it flatly: they had neither legal nor constitutional right to call another man to the throne, Jeroboam being no kin to the royal house, and nothing could justify the act but the just judgment of God, who thus punished a gainsaying people, and especially Solomon’s family. John Gill (reformed) agrees that it is rightly called a rebellion: though it was according to the will of God, the people had no order from God for it, did it without consulting him, and so rejected their lawful prince. Ellicott hears the other side’s case in their title: king over all Israel indicates a claim by the ten tribes to be the true Israel, relying perhaps on the prophetic choice of Jeroboam and professing to have risen in the Lord’s name against the idolatry of Solomon’s house.

The prophet who stops the war is the chapter’s hinge. Ellicott observes that while the prophet of the original promise belonged to Shiloh in Ephraim, Shemaiah was attached to Judah, which makes his interference to protect the new kingdom the more striking; to it the preservation of Jeroboam’s half-formed kingdom was probably due, and it indicates the great opportunity given that kingdom to maintain itself under God’s blessing, a point the phrase your brethren, the children of Israel, marks with emphasis. Keil and Delitzsch note that Shemaiah is not mentioned again, and gloss the divine reason, with Schmidt, as Rehoboam’s being deprived of sovereignty over ten tribes, not the rebellion itself. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) admires both halves of the king’s conduct: it was brave to design reducing the revolters by force, braver to desist when ordered to lay down his arms; he would not lose a kingdom tamely, for then he were unworthy the title of a prince, nor contend for it against God, for then he were unworthy the title of an Israelite. Clarke calls the compliance great deference in king and officers alike, and notes that the people heard the command gratefully, since the mass of mankind are averse from war, and no nations would rise against each other were they not instigated or compelled by their rulers.
25:
The new king’s first care is fortification, his second religion. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) traces the vicissitudes of the capital he chose: a city already when Abraham entered the land, then the seat of Abimelech’s usurpation and destroyed for rebelling against him, so that building it may mean rebuilding it or only fortifying it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) give the motive: to strengthen his kingdom internally he provided a substitute for the temple’s sacrificial worship, removing all occasion for festal journeys to Jerusalem, from which he apprehended, probably not without reason, a return of the people and danger to his own life. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) locates the fault deeper: a practical disbelief of God’s all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all our treacherous departures from him.

What the calves were meant to be is agreed in law, disputed in origin. Henry insists they were made to represent, or rather make present, not any false god but the God of Israel himself, so that the offence was against the second commandment and not the first; and he supposes Jeroboam adopted the Egyptian worship of a god under the figure of a bull. Ellicott finds several causes at work: the repetition of Aaron’s words marks it as a revival of the ancient idolatry of the wilderness, the Egyptian animal worship had been lately familiar to Jeroboam, and there is reason to think the cherubim were winged bulls, so that the calves may be reproductions of them, made symbols not of the natural powers obeying the divine word but of the Deity itself. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls the whole an invented political religion, and finds it strange that in pointing out his calves the king used Aaron’s very words.

The two sites were chosen as frontiers and kept for their memories. Ellicott notes that Bethel preserved in its name the memory of Jacob’s vision and his consecration of the place, and had been a place of religious assembly and perhaps of the ark’s occasional sojourn, while at Dan the sanctuary set up by the Danites at the conquest probably lingered, so that the priests of that old worship became the natural ministers of the new. John Gill (reformed) gives the same reason for Bethel more plainly: its very name signifies the house of God. Henry reads the placing as policy: Bethel lay close to Judah, to tempt such of Rehoboam’s subjects as were inclined to image-worship, and Dan served those most remote; and by setting up two he would break them by degrees off the unity of the godhead. Clarke sees the ground prepared already, since Solomon’s own idolatry had made the people ready for these abominations.

The priesthood and the calendar were altered to match. Clarke explains the house of high places as a temple of temples, one chief sanctuary over the many, with a priesthood of Jeroboam’s own ordination: he took the people as they came, not troubling himself whether they were of Aaron’s family, for any priests would do well enough for such gods, and probably the sons of Levi had grace to refuse. Henry puts it in a phrase: the lowest of the people were good enough to be priests to his calves, and too good. On the month, Keil and Delitzsch allow him a pretext, that in the north the corn ripened later than in Judah, and Gill reports the same from Abarbinel, adding that he might hope for a fuller attendance once all was gathered in. Ellicott calls the choice of day characteristic: it challenged likeness to the feast that was in Judah and yet took liberty to alter the date, assuming the right to set aside the letter of the old law while still professing to worship Jehovah.
